{"parentUuid":"4390213a-75b0-4892-be2b-76fbef6c1824","isSidechain":false,"message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_011CgGLRFD3uwcGaNuQeXXDe","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The app already behaved this way, so no app code changed. I added `tests/test_login_hardening.py`, which pins the behavior down.\n\n**What I found:** `app/routes/auth.py:14` already gives a wrong password, an unknown email and a deactivated account the same message (`LOGIN_ERROR`) and a 401. `accounts.authenticate` also runs the slow password check for unknown emails, so response time doesn't reveal which emails have accounts.\n\n**The test:** `test_wrong_password_and_unknown_email_get_the_same_response` posts to `/login` once with the admin's email and a wrong password, and once with an unknown email. It checks two things:\n- **Status:** both responses return 401.\n- **Message:** the error shown on each page is identical, and equals the literal `\"Incorrect email or password.\"`. The expected text is written into the test rather than imported from `LOGIN_ERROR`, so changing that constant can't make the test pass by accident.\n\nIt compares the displayed error rather than the whole page, because the page shows the typed email back to the user and so always differs between the two cases.\n\n**Can it fail?** It passed as soon as it was written, so I broke the app on purpose twice, put it back each time, and confirmed the test caught both:\n- Unknown email returns a 404: the test fails with `assert 401 == 404`.\n- Unknown email shows \"No such account.\": the test fails on the message comparison.\n\n`app/routes/auth.py` is back to its committed state. The full suite passes: `uv run pytest -q` gives 213 passed (212 before, plus this test).\n\nNothing is committed. Your checklist commits S2 after the rate-limit prompt and `/code-review`. When you stage, include only `tests/test_login_hardening.py` and leave `CONTEXT.md` and ADR-006 for P3."}],"container":null,"stop_reason":"end_turn","stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":359,"cache_read_input_tokens":49561,"output_tokens":623,"output_tokens_details":{"thinking_tokens":28},"server_tool_use":{"web_search_requests":0,"web_fetch_requests":0},"service_tier":"standard","cache_creation":{"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":359,"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":0},"inference_geo":"global","iterations":[{"input_tokens":2,"output_tokens":623,"cache_read_input_tokens":49561,"cache_creation_input_tokens":359,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":0,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":359},"type":"message"}],"speed":"standard","fallback_credit":null},"input_transformations":[],"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"serverClassifierRequest":"970abe68-0461-497f-99cc-468ee0a84b09","apiBlockIndex":1,"requestId":"req_011CgGLREPSyeBD86FCHHuGy","requestRef":"c325016d-8f18-4a09-8109-9f10fc4277b2","requestedModel":"claude-opus-5-5","attributionSkill":"mattpocock-skills:tdd","attributionPlugin":"mattpocock-skills","type":"assistant","uuid":"88826c62-7128-441e-a3ba-54effe604371","timestamp":"2026-10-22T00:33:33.271Z","advisorModel":"claude-opus-5-5","effort":"medium","perTurnEffort":"medium","session_id":"e68901dd-4f60-40d0-873c-0a5584ccf73d","userType":"external","entrypoint":"cli","cwd":"/home/refiv/ubuncode/iphs400-mp2-cms","sessionId":"2cc1b141-f6f4-406d-a6f6-e0223c5e422f","version":"2.1.307","gitBranch":"main"}

{"parentUuid":"950d0296-eeff-4fb5-a373-e29df6edec1e","isSidechain":false,"promptId":"c77ca216-bd4d-4e75-851f-890b4ee040ca","type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":"<command-message>mattpocock-skills:tdd</command-message>\n<command-name>/mattpocock-skills:tdd</command-name>\n<command-args>Rate-limit login, keyed on the account: after 5 failed attempts for one email within 15 minutes, refuse further attempts for that email with 429 and the login page showing a lockout message, even with the right password. Count failures by the typed email, trimmed and lowercased, including emails with no account or a deactivated one. A successful login clears that email's failures. Keep failures in one module-level limiter in memory with a clock attribute (time.monotonic by default) so tests can freeze and advance it. Ordinary failures stay 401 with LOGIN_ERROR. In tests/test_login_hardening.py, test that attempt 6 is refused, that a login works again once 15 minutes have passed, and that another email can still log in from the same client. Add an autouse fixture reset_limiter to tests/conftest.py that clears the limiter and restores the real clock; change nothing else in conftest. No new dependencies. See docs/adr/ADR-006-login-limiter-in-memory.md.</command-args>"},"uuid":"7ffd7872-1990-4de7-a4f3-e8d6fc9f808b","timestamp":"2026-10-22T00:35:00.400Z","origin":{"kind":"human"},"turnOrigin":"human","turnPosition":{"promptIndex":2,"turnIndex":2},"userType":"external","entrypoint":"cli","cwd":"/home/refiv/ubuncode/iphs400-mp2-cms","sessionId":"2cc1b141-f6f4-406d-a6f6-e0223c5e422f","version":"2.1.307","gitBranch":"main"}
{"parentUuid":"7ffd7872-1990-4de7-a4f3-e8d6fc9f808b","isSidechain":false,"promptId":"c77ca216-bd4d-4e75-851f-890b4ee040ca","type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: /home/refiv/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/mattpocock-skills/1.2.3/skills/engineering/tdd\n\n# Test-Driven Development\n\nTDD is the red → green loop. This skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle: consult them before and during the loop, not after.\n\nWhen exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.\n\n## What a good test is\n\nTests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely; tests shouldn't. A good test reads like a specification: \"user can checkout with valid cart\" tells you exactly what capability exists, and it survives refactors because it doesn't care about internal structure.\n\nSee [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for mocking guidelines.\n\n## Seams: where tests go\n\nA **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.\n\n**Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything, so agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.\n\nAsk: \"What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?\"\n\nWhen the shape of that interface is itself in question (how deep the module is, where the seam belongs, what the interface should expose), call the Skill tool with \"codebase-design\" for the vocabulary. It is the shared source of the module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage and locality terms, and it is a reference to consult, not a session to run.\n\n## Anti-patterns\n\n- **Implementation-coupled**: mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (querying the database instead of using the interface). The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed.\n- **Tautological**: the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does (`expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`, a snapshot derived by hand the same way, a constant asserted equal to itself), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code. Expected values must come from an independent source of truth: a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.\n- **Horizontal slicing**: writing all tests first, then all implementation. Bulk tests verify _imagined_ behavior: you test the _shape_ of things rather than user-facing behavior, the tests go insensitive to real changes, and you commit to test structure before understanding the implementation. Work in **vertical slices** instead: one test → one implementation → repeat, each test a **tracer bullet** that responds to what the last cycle taught you.\n\n## Rules of the loop\n\n- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.\n- **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.\n- **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.\n\n\nARGUMENTS: Rate-limit login, keyed on the account: after 5 failed attempts for one email within 15 minutes, refuse further attempts for that email with 429 and the login page showing a lockout message, even with the right password. Count failures by the typed email, trimmed and lowercased, including emails with no account or a deactivated one. A successful login clears that email's failures. Keep failures in one module-level limiter in memory with a clock attribute (time.monotonic by default) so tests can freeze and advance it. Ordinary failures stay 401 with LOGIN_ERROR. In tests/test_login_hardening.py, test that attempt 6 is refused, that a login works again once 15 minutes have passed, and that another email can still log in from the same client. Add an autouse fixture reset_limiter to tests/conftest.py that clears the limiter and restores the real clock; change nothing else in conftest. No new dependencies. See docs/adr/ADR-006-login-limiter-in-memory.md."}]},"isMeta":true,"turnCompanion":true,"uuid":"7d6f939b-3f30-4df8-8d2e-b5e1d95b0b77","timestamp":"2026-10-22T00:35:00.400Z","userType":"external","entrypoint":"cli","cwd":"/home/refiv/ubuncode/iphs400-mp2-cms","sessionId":"2cc1b141-f6f4-406d-a6f6-e0223c5e422f","version":"2.1.307","gitBranch":"main"}

{"type":"api-request-blob","sessionId":"2cc1b141-f6f4-406d-a6f6-e0223c5e422f","hash":"b57e36b764ed712c9f0e3b24b1839ed7649337a7c06f202fbcf4a892b5728f85","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"<command-message>mattpocock-skills:tdd</command-message>\n<command-name>/mattpocock-skills:tdd</command-name>\n<command-args>Rate-limit login, keyed on the account: after 5 failed attempts for one email within 15 minutes, refuse further attempts for that email with 429 and the login page showing a lockout message, even with the right password. Count failures by the typed email, trimmed and lowercased, including emails with no account or a deactivated one. A successful login clears that email's failures. Keep failures in one module-level limiter in memory with a clock attribute (time.monotonic by default) so tests can freeze and advance it. Ordinary failures stay 401 with LOGIN_ERROR. In tests/test_login_hardening.py, test that attempt 6 is refused, that a login works again once 15 minutes have passed, and that another email can still log in from the same client. Add an autouse fixture reset_limiter to tests/conftest.py that clears the limiter and restores the real clock; change nothing else in conftest. No new dependencies. See docs/adr/ADR-006-login-limiter-in-memory.md.</command-args>\n"},{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: /home/refiv/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/mattpocock-skills/1.2.3/skills/engineering/tdd\n\n# Test-Driven Development\n\nTDD is the red → green loop. This skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle: consult them before and during the loop, not after.\n\nWhen exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.\n\n## What a good test is\n\nTests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely; tests shouldn't. A good test reads like a specification: \"user can checkout with valid cart\" tells you exactly what capability exists, and it survives refactors because it doesn't care about internal structure.\n\nSee [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for mocking guidelines.\n\n## Seams: where tests go\n\nA **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.\n\n**Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything, so agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.\n\nAsk: \"What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?\"\n\nWhen the shape of that interface is itself in question (how deep the module is, where the seam belongs, what the interface should expose), call the Skill tool with \"codebase-design\" for the vocabulary. It is the shared source of the module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage and locality terms, and it is a reference to consult, not a session to run.\n\n## Anti-patterns\n\n- **Implementation-coupled**: mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (querying the database instead of using the interface). The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed.\n- **Tautological**: the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does (`expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`, a snapshot derived by hand the same way, a constant asserted equal to itself), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code. Expected values must come from an independent source of truth: a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.\n- **Horizontal slicing**: writing all tests first, then all implementation. Bulk tests verify _imagined_ behavior: you test the _shape_ of things rather than user-facing behavior, the tests go insensitive to real changes, and you commit to test structure before understanding the implementation. Work in **vertical slices** instead: one test → one implementation → repeat, each test a **tracer bullet** that responds to what the last cycle taught you.\n\n## Rules of the loop\n\n- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.\n- **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.\n- **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.\n\n\nARGUMENTS: Rate-limit login, keyed on the account: after 5 failed attempts for one email within 15 minutes, refuse further attempts for that email with 429 and the login page showing a lockout message, even with the right password. Count failures by the typed email, trimmed and lowercased, including emails with no account or a deactivated one. A successful login clears that email's failures. Keep failures in one module-level limiter in memory with a clock attribute (time.monotonic by default) so tests can freeze and advance it. Ordinary failures stay 401 with LOGIN_ERROR. In tests/test_login_hardening.py, test that attempt 6 is refused, that a login works again once 15 minutes have passed, and that another email can still log in from the same client. Add an autouse fixture reset_limiter to tests/conftest.py that clears the limiter and restores the real clock; change nothing else in conftest. No new dependencies. See docs/adr/ADR-006-login-limiter-in-memory.md."}]}}

{"parentUuid":"709ea888-53d4-41bb-ba8e-9154a90d1a6d","isSidechain":false,"promptId":"c77ca216-bd4d-4e75-851f-890b4ee040ca","type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_018aN1nXv2vgwYezzXhJ9CxZ","type":"tool_result","content":"# ADR-006: The login limiter keeps failed logins in memory\n\n**Status:** proposed (draft; accept once S2's limiter is in the code)\n**Date:** 2026-10-21\n\n## Context\n\nChecklist #2 and MP2plus S2: after 5 failed logins for one email within 15\nminutes, the next attempt is refused with 429, even with the right password.\nThe count has to live somewhere. The console runs as one process on the one\nteam laptop (`cms serve`), and the schema in `app/db.py` is only ever created,\nnever migrated: a new table means `rm cms.db` and a reseed on that laptop.\nOptions considered: a `failed_logins` table in `cms.db`, a limiter on\n`app.state` (one per app), and one limiter object in its own module.\n\n## Decision\n\nOne module-level limiter holds, per typed email (trimmed, lowercased), the\ntimes of its recent failed logins. It reads the time through a `clock`\nattribute (`time.monotonic` by default), so tests can freeze and advance it.\nA successful login clears that email's failures. The autouse fixture\n`reset_limiter` in `tests/conftest.py` clears it and restores the real clock\nbefore every test.\n\nRejected: a `failed_logins` table, which survives restarts but costs a schema\nchange and a reseed, and is already reset by each test's fresh database;\nand `app.state`, because the `login_as` fixture builds a new app per client,\nso failures would not carry from one client to the next.\n\n## Consequences\n\n- No schema change and no reseed for S2.\n- Restarting the console clears every lockout. Only someone who can already\n  restart the team laptop gains from that; accepted.\n- Running more than one server process would split the count. On one laptop\n  there is one process; moving off it means revisiting this ADR.\n- Tests share one limiter, so the autouse fixture is what keeps the 212\n  existing tests from tripping a 429.\n19:**Lockout**:\n20:The 15 minutes during which an email that has had 5 failed logins is refused, even with the right password. A successful login before the lockout clears the count; the lockout ends on its own.\n121:| What does the login limiter count by? | The typed email, including emails with no account, not the IP address | All posting happens on one team laptop, so an IP limit would lock out the Coach whenever someone else on it mistyped; and counting unknown emails too means the 429 can't tell anyone which emails have accounts (checklist #2). |\n\n    return _find\n\n\n@pytest.fixture\ndef new_account(client_as, post_form):\n    \"\"\"Return a helper: new_account(email, password, role) creates it as the admin.\n\n    Goes through the admin's account-management route, like the Coach would.\n    \"\"\"\n    admin = None\n\n    def _create(email: str, password: str, role: Role = Role.EDITOR) -> None:\n        nonlocal admin\n        admin = admin or client_as(\"admin\")\n        response = post_form(admin, \"/admin/accounts\", email=email,\n                             password=password, role=role)\n        assert response.status_code == 303, response.text\n\n    return _create","is_error":false}]},"uuid":"d600adf5-d5f8-45ae-9d23-67f45441160f","timestamp":"2026-10-22T00:35:02.419Z","toolUseResult":{"stdout":"# ADR-006: The login limiter keeps failed logins in memory\n\n**Status:** proposed (draft; accept once S2's limiter is in the code)\n**Date:** 2026-10-21\n\n## Context\n\nChecklist #2 and MP2plus S2: after 5 failed logins for one email within 15\nminutes, the next attempt is refused with 429, even with the right password.\nThe count has to live somewhere. Next I'll write the smallest limiter that makes it pass, with no time handling yet, plus the fixture that clears it."},{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_01EWxWs6hgGoFxNYm6MdDDu3","name":"Bash","input":{"command":"cd /home/refiv/ubuncode/iphs400-mp2-cms && cat > app/login_limiter.py <<'EOF'\n\"\"\"Refuses logins for an email after too many failures (ADR-006).\"\"\"\nfrom __future__ import annotations\n\nMAX_FAILURES = 5\n\n\nclass LoginLimiter:\n    \"\"\"Counts failed logins per typed email, kept in memory.\"\"\"\n\n    def __init__(self) -> None:\n        self._failures: dict[str, int] = {}\n\n    def is_locked(self, email: str) -> bool:\n        return self._failures.get(_key(email), 0) >= MAX_FAILURES\n\n    def record_failure(self, email: str) -> None:\n        key = _key(email)\n        self._failures[key] = self._failures.get(key, 0) + 1\n\n    def reset(self) -> None:\n        self._failures.clear()\n\n\ndef _key(email: str) -> str:\n    return email.strip().lower()\n\n\nlimiter = LoginLimiter()\nEOF\npython3 - <<'EOF'\nimport re\np=\"app/routes/auth.py\"; s=open(p).read()\ns=s.replace(\"from app import accounts\\n\",\"from app import accounts\\nfrom app.login_limiter import limiter\\n\")\ns=s.replace('''LOGIN_ERROR = \"Incorrect email or password.\"\n''','''LOGIN_ERROR = \"Incorrect email or password.\"\nLOCKOUT_ERROR = \"Too many failed logins. Try again in 15 minutes.\"\n''')\ns=s.replace('''def login(request: Request, email: str = Form(\"\"), password: str = Form(\"\")):\n    account = accounts.authenticate(request.app.state.db_path, email, password)\n    if account is None:\n        return templates.TemplateResponse(\n            request, \"admin/login.html\",\n            {\"title\": \"Log in\", \"email\": email, \"error\": LOGIN_ERROR},\n            status_code=401,\n        )\n''','''def login(request: Request, email: str = Form(\"\"), password: str = Form(\"\")):\n    if limiter.is_locked(email):\n        return _login_page(request, email, LOCKOUT_ERROR, status_code=429)\n    account = accounts.authenticate(request.app.state.db_path, email, password)\n    if account is None:\n        limiter.record_failure(email)\n        return _login_page(request, email, LOGIN_ERROR, status_code=401)\n''')\ns=s.replace('''@router.post(\"/logout\"''','''def _login_page(request: Request, email: str, error: str, status_code: int):\n    return templates.TemplateResponse(\n        request, \"admin/login.html\",\n        {\"title\": \"Log in\", \"email\": email, \"error\": error},\n        status_code=status_code,\n    )\n\n\n@router.post(\"/logout\"''')\nopen(p,\"w\").write(s)\np=\"tests/conftest.py\"; s=open(p).read()\ns=s.replace(\"from app.deploy import DeployFailed\\n\",\"from app.deploy import DeployFailed\\nfrom app.login_limiter import limiter\\n\")\ns+='''\n\n@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)\ndef reset_limiter():\n    \"\"\"Every test starts with no failed logins counted (ADR-006).\"\"\"\n    limiter.reset()\n'''\nopen(p,\"w\").write(s)\nEOF\ngit diff app/routes/auth.py | head -60; uv run pytest -q tests/test_login_hardening.py 2>&1 | tail -1"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}]}}

{"parentUuid":"f839cd13-f59f-4d46-be51-b47b564572b6","isSidechain":false,"message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_011CgGLyjptFQVMeaQdE7r26","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Login is now rate-limited per email: after 5 failed attempts within 15 minutes, that email gets a 429 and a lockout message, even with the right password. The full suite passes (`uv run pytest -q`: 217 passed) and `check_submission.py --stage 2` reports 22/22.\n\n**What changed**\n- **`app/login_limiter.py` (new):** one module-level `limiter` that keeps failed logins in memory, keyed on the typed email trimmed and lowercased. It reads the time through a `clock` attribute (`time.monotonic` by default). Emails with no account and deactivated accounts are counted the same way, because every failed login is counted.\n- **`app/routes/auth.py`:** a locked email gets 429 with \"Too many failed logins. Try again in 15 minutes.\" Ordinary failures still get 401 with `LOGIN_ERROR`. A successful login clears that email's failures.\n- **`tests/conftest.py`:** only the `reset_limiter` fixture (autouse) and the two imports it needs. It clears the limiter and puts the real clock back before every test.\n- **`tests/test_login_hardening.py`:** the three tests you asked for, plus a fourth: \"a successful login clears that email's failures\". None of the three exercised that rule, so I added a test before writing the code for it rather than leave it untested.\n\n**How the tests were checked**\n- Every test except the different-email one failed before its code was written.\n- The different-email test passed straight away, since the limiter already keys on email. I broke the limiter so it ignored the email, and that test failed, so it does catch the problem it's meant to.\n\n**A choice you might want to change:** the lockout lasts 15 minutes from the 5th failure, matching the \"Lockout\" definition in `CONTEXT.md`. The other reading of \"5 within 15 minutes\" would end the lockout 15 minutes after the *first* of the five failures. The current tests pass either way, because every failure happens at the same frozen time.\n\n**Not tested:** that \" Editor@X \" and \"editor@x\" count as the same email. The code trims and lowercases, but no test checks it.\n\n**Next:** run `/code-review`, then commit with an `S2:` message and stage only `app/login_limiter.py`, `app/routes/auth.py`, `tests/conftest.py` and `tests/test_login_hardening.py`. Leave `CONTEXT.md` and ADR-006 for P3. The user can send it another message and resume it, so the same task-id may notify more than once.</note>\n<result>I found 7 issues in the login-limiter change. The most serious is a race: an attacker sending many login requests at once can make far more than 5 password guesses for one email. I only read the code; I didn't run the tests.\n\n```json\n[\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/routes/auth.py\",\n    \"line\": 27,\n    \"summary\": \"Check-then-act race: `is_locked` runs before the slow argon2 `authenticate`, and `record_failure` runs only after it. `def login` is a sync route, so FastAPI runs requests in its threadpool and concurrent guesses all pass the lock check before any failure is recorded.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"An attacker sends 40 POSTs to /login for the Coach's email at the same moment (default threadpool is about 40 workers). All 40 see `is_locked() == False` and each gets a full password verification, so one burst gets 40 guesses instead of the 5 allowed. Repeat after every lockout.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/login_limiter.py\",\n    \"line\": 27,\n    \"summary\": \"`record_failure` is a read-modify-write on shared dicts (`get`, then build a list, then assign) with no lock, while running in threadpool threads; concurrent failures for the same email overwrite each other.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"Two failed logins for the same email finish at the same time. Both read the same list of 4 failures, and each writes back its own list of 5, so one failure is lost. Or thread A sets `_locked_until` and clears the list while thread B writes back a stale list of 4, leaving the count wrong after the lockout. Either way the 5-failure rule is enforced unreliably.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/login_limiter.py\",\n    \"line\": 30,\n    \"summary\": \"Memory grows without limit: every distinct typed email, including emails with no account (counted on purpose), gets a permanent `_failures` key, and `_locked_until` entries are never removed after they expire. Nothing ever prunes either dict.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"A script posts failed logins with millions of random emails (it only needs a CSRF token). Each adds a dict key with a list that is never freed, so the console's memory grows until it is restarted. Expired lockouts also stay in `_locked_until` for good.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/login_limiter.py\",\n    \"line\": 35,\n    \"summary\": \"`clear()` removes `_failures` but leaves `_locked_until`. This works only because the route checks `is_locked` first; any other caller, such as a future password reset or an admin unlock, would not lift the lockout.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"Once the code calls `limiter.clear(email)` to unlock an account, for example after the Coach resets a captain's password, the captain still gets 429 until the 15 minutes are up, because the `_locked_until` entry stays.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/routes/auth.py\",\n    \"line\": 16,\n    \"summary\": \"`LOCKOUT_ERROR` has \\\"15 minutes\\\" written into the text instead of being built from `login_limiter.WINDOW`, so the message and the real lockout length can disagree.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"Someone changes `WINDOW` to 30*60. Users are still told to wait 15 minutes, get 429 again after 15, and conclude the console is broken. The test also hardcodes the text, so it would not catch the mismatch.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/login_limiter.py\",\n    \"line\": 44,\n    \"summary\": \"`_key()` copies `app.accounts._normalize` (`email.strip().lower()`) instead of calling it, so the two rules for normalising an email can drift apart.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"If `accounts._normalize` later adds Unicode NFKC folding, the same account could be reached through variants the limiter counts as different emails, each with its own 5 guesses, which bypasses the per-email limit. One shared function avoids this.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/routes/auth.py\",\n    \"line\": 27,\n    \"summary\": \"The rate limiting sits in the route as three separate calls (`is_locked`, `record_failure`, `clear`) around `authenticate`. It could instead be one operation that checks, verifies and records together, which would also fix the race above.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"Any second login path, such as a re-authentication prompt or a CLI login, has to remember all three calls in the right order. Forgetting `record_failure` there gives unlimited guesses. Wrapping them, for example as `accounts.authenticate_limited(...)` returning ok / bad / locked under a per-email lock, keeps the rule in one place.\"\n  }\n]\n```</result>\n<usage><subagent_tokens>42131</subagent_tokens><tool_uses>3</tool_uses><duration_ms>31468</duration_ms></usage>\n</task-notification>"}

The user can send it another message and resume it, so the same task-id may notify more than once.</note>\n<result>I found 7 issues in the login-limiter change. The most serious is a race: an attacker sending many login requests at once can make far more than 5 password guesses for one email. I only read the code; I didn't run the tests.\n\n```json\n[\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/routes/auth.py\",\n    \"line\": 27,\n    \"summary\": \"Check-then-act race: `is_locked` runs before the slow argon2 `authenticate`, and `record_failure` runs only after it. `def login` is a sync route, so FastAPI runs requests in its threadpool and concurrent guesses all pass the lock check before any failure is recorded.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"An attacker sends 40 POSTs to /login for the Coach's email at the same moment (default threadpool is about 40 workers). All 40 see `is_locked() == False` and each gets a full password verification, so one burst gets 40 guesses instead of the 5 allowed. Repeat after every lockout.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/login_limiter.py\",\n    \"line\": 27,\n    \"summary\": \"`record_failure` is a read-modify-write on shared dicts (`get`, then build a list, then assign) with no lock, while running in threadpool threads; concurrent failures for the same email overwrite each other.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"Two failed logins for the same email finish at the same time. Both read the same list of 4 failures, and each writes back its own list of 5, so one failure is lost. Or thread A sets `_locked_until` and clears the list while thread B writes back a stale list of 4, leaving the count wrong after the lockout. Either way the 5-failure rule is enforced unreliably.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/login_limiter.py\",\n    \"line\": 30,\n    \"summary\": \"Memory grows without limit: every distinct typed email, including emails with no account (counted on purpose), gets a permanent `_failures` key, and `_locked_until` entries are never removed after they expire. Nothing ever prunes either dict.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"A script posts failed logins with millions of random emails (it only needs a CSRF token). Each adds a dict key with a list that is never freed, so the console's memory grows until it is restarted. Expired lockouts also stay in `_locked_until` for good.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/login_limiter.py\",\n    \"line\": 35,\n    \"summary\": \"`clear()` removes `_failures` but leaves `_locked_until`. This works only because the route checks `is_locked` first; any other caller, such as a future password reset or an admin unlock, would not lift the lockout.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"Once the code calls `limiter.clear(email)` to unlock an account, for example after the Coach resets a captain's password, the captain still gets 429 until the 15 minutes are up, because the `_locked_until` entry stays.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/routes/auth.py\",\n    \"line\": 16,\n    \"summary\": \"`LOCKOUT_ERROR` has \\\"15 minutes\\\" written into the text instead of being built from `login_limiter.WINDOW`, so the message and the real lockout length can disagree.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"Someone changes `WINDOW` to 30*60. Users are still told to wait 15 minutes, get 429 again after 15, and conclude the console is broken. The test also hardcodes the text, so it would not catch the mismatch.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/login_limiter.py\",\n    \"line\": 44,\n    \"summary\": \"`_key()` copies `app.accounts._normalize` (`email.strip().lower()`) instead of calling it, so the two rules for normalising an email can drift apart.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"If `accounts._normalize` later adds Unicode NFKC folding, the same account could be reached through variants the limiter counts as different emails, each with its own 5 guesses, which bypasses the per-email limit. One shared function avoids this.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/routes/auth.py\",\n    \"line\": 27,\n    \"summary\": \"The rate limiting sits in the route as three separate calls (`is_locked`, `record_failure`, `clear`) around `authenticate`. It could instead be one operation that checks, verifies and records together, which would also fix the race above.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"Any second login path, such as a re-authentication prompt or a CLI login, has to remember all three calls in the right order. Forgetting `record_failure` there gives unlimited guesses. Wrapping them, for example as `accounts.authenticate_limited(...)` returning ok / bad / locked under a per-email lock, keeps the rule in one place.\"\n  }\n]\n```</result>\n<usage><subagent_tokens>42131</subagent_tokens><tool_uses>3</tool_uses><duration_ms>31468</duration_ms></usage>\n</task-notification>"},"uuid":"6ec95b34-8737-40b0-96fc-d942907b2785","timestamp":"2026-10-22T00:42:37.158Z","permissionMode":"auto","origin":{"kind":"task-notification","producer":"session-task","runId":"0mvitgau3-15701677"},"promptSource":"system","turnOrigin":"task_notification","turnPosition":{"promptIndex":2,"turnIndex":3},"queueSkipAttachments":true,"userType":"external","entrypoint":"cli","cwd":"/home/refiv/ubuncode/iphs400-mp2-cms","sessionId":"2cc1b141-f6f4-406d-a6f6-e0223c5e422f","version":"2.1.307","gitBranch":"main"}

{"parentUuid":"4871ace5-0a4d-45dd-8454-e1ff65223feb","isSidechain":false,"promptId":"5bbd487b-5c27-4107-99cb-5ac0e6ca5c8e","type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: /home/refiv/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/mattpocock-skills/1.2.3/skills/engineering/ask-matt\n\n# Ask Matt\n\nYou don't remember every skill, so ask.\n\nA **flow** is a path through the skills. Most paths run along one **main flow**, and two **on-ramps** merge onto it. Everything else is standalone, or a vocabulary layer that runs underneath.\n\n## The main flow: idea → ship\n\nThe route most work travels. You have an idea and want it built.\n\n1. **`/grill-with-docs`** sharpens the idea by interview. Start here whenever you are **working in a working directory**: it's stateful, retaining what it learns in `CONTEXT.md` and ADRs. (No working directory? Use `/grill-me` instead, covered under Standalone. Both run the same `/grilling` primitive; `grill-with-docs` is the one that leaves a paper trail, which makes it the better of the two whenever a repo is there to leave it in.)\n2. **Branch: can you settle every question in conversation?** If a question needs a runnable answer (state, business logic, a UI you have to see), detour through a prototype, bridged by **`/handoff`** in both directions (a prototype lives in its own directory, which is exactly what `/handoff` is for; see Phase boundaries):\n   - **`/handoff`** out, then open a fresh session against that file,\n   - **`/prototype`** to answer the question with throwaway code,\n   - **`/handoff`** back what you learned, and reference it from the original idea thread.\n3. **Branch: is this a multi-session build?**\n   - **Yes** → **`/to-spec`** (turn the thread into a spec), then **`/to-tickets`** to split it into tracer-bullet tickets, each declaring its **blocking edges**. On a local tracker that's one file per ticket under `.scratch/<feature>/issues/`, worked blockers-first by hand; on a real tracker the edges become native blocking links, so any ticket whose blockers are done can be grabbed: kick off **`/implement`** per ticket, **`/clear`ing context between each one**. Each ticket is self-contained, so the last one's context is disposable.\n   - **No** → **`/implement`** right here, in the same context window.\n\n   Either way, **`/implement`** builds each issue by driving **`/tdd`** internally (one red-green slice at a time), then closes out by running **`/code-review`**, a two-axis review (Standards + Spec) of the diff, before committing. Reach for **`/tdd`** on its own when you just want to build a concrete behaviour test-first without a full spec, and **`/code-review`** on its own whenever you want to review a branch or PR against a fixed point.\n\n### Context hygiene\n\nKeep steps 1–3 in **one unbroken context window** (don't compact or clear until after `/to-tickets`) so the grilling, spec, and tickets all build on the same thinking. Each `/implement` then starts fresh, working from the ticket.\n\nThe limit on this is the **[smart zone](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/smart-zone)**: the window (~150k tokens on state-of-the-art models) within which the model still reasons sharply. If a session approaches it before `/to-tickets`, don't push on degraded; `/compact` at the nearest phase boundary and carry on (see Phase boundaries).\n\n## On-ramps\n\nA starting situation that generates work, then merges onto the main flow.\n\n- **Bugs and requests piling up** → **`/triage`**. It moves issues through triage roles and produces agent-ready issues, which **`/implement`** later picks up.\n\n  Triage is only for issues **you didn't create**: bug reports, incoming feature requests, anything that arrives raw. Tickets that `/to-tickets` produced are already agent-ready, so **don't triage them**.\n\n- **Something's broken** → **`/diagnosing-bugs`**. For the hard ones: the bug that resists a first glance, the intermittent flake, the regression that crept in between two known-good states. It refuses to theorise until it has a **tight feedback loop** (one command that already goes red on *this* bug), then fixes with a regression test. Its post-mortem hands off to **`/improve-codebase-architecture`** when the real finding is that there's no good seam to lock the bug down.\n\n- **A huge, foggy effort: a greenfield project or a huge feature build, too big for one session** → **`/wayfinder`**, the most cognitively demanding flow here. When the way from here to the destination isn't visible yet, it charts a **shared map** of **decision tickets** on the issue tracker and resolves them one at a time, producing **decisions, not deliverables**, until the fog is pushed back and the way is clear. Where **`/grill-with-docs`** sharpens an idea you can hold in one session, wayfinder is for the idea you can't, and it's slower and denser, so save it for exactly that, never a well-scoped feature.\n\n  When the map clears, **it hands off, it doesn't build**: merge onto the main flow at **`/to-spec`**, which collapses the map's linked decisions into a buildable plan, then `/to-tickets` and `/implement` as usual. Looping the map straight into `/implement` skips that collapse and throws the linked detail away, so go straight to `/implement` only when the effort turned out genuinely small.\n\n## Codebase health\n\nNot feature work, just upkeep.\n\n- **`/improve-codebase-architecture`** runs whenever you have a spare moment to keep the codebase good for agents to operate in. It surfaces **deepening opportunities**; picking one _generates an idea_ you can take into the main flow at `/grill-with-docs`. It's the survey that finds the candidates; **`/codebase-design`** (below) is the bench you design the chosen one on.\n\n## Vocabulary underneath\n\nTwo model-invoked references that run *beneath* the other skills, each the single source of truth for its vocabulary. Reach for them directly when the **words**, not the process, are the problem; or let the skills above pull them in.\n\n- **`/domain-modeling`**: sharpen the project's *domain* language: challenge a fuzzy term, resolve an overloaded word (\"account\" doing three jobs), record a hard-to-reverse decision as an ADR. It's the active discipline `/grill-with-docs` drives to keep `CONTEXT.md` a clean glossary.\n- **`/codebase-design`** is the deep-module vocabulary (module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage, locality) for designing a module's *shape*: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface at a clean seam. `/tdd` and `/improve-codebase-architecture` both speak it.\n\n## Phase boundaries\n\nA **phase** is a chunk of work inside a session: the grilling, the implementation, the QA. At the **boundary** between two of them you have five options, and picking between them is the fuzziest decision in this whole map:\n\n- **Continue**: stay put. Costs nothing, loses nothing.\n- **`/clear`**: empty the window, when nothing here matters to what's next.\n- **`/handoff`** writes a portable markdown file. Narrow: only for a **new harness**, a **new directory**, a **colleague**, or forking a side task **mid-phase**. What it buys is portability.\n- **Subagent**: send a tightly-scoped task to its own window and get a report back.\n- **`/compact`** compresses this context and seeds a fresh session with it. The **default**, at the bottom of the tree rather than the first reach.\n\nRead [PHASE-BOUNDARIES.md](PHASE-BOUNDARIES.md) for the ordered tree: the five questions, the reasoning behind each branch, and why the primary-source cost makes **Continue** the one to rule out first. Make the decision **at** a boundary; mid-phase, continue or split the rest into subagents.\n\n## Standalone\n\nOff the main flow entirely.\n\n- **`/grill-me`**: the same relentless interview as `/grill-with-docs`, but **stateless**: it saves nothing locally and builds no `CONTEXT.md`. Reach for it when you are **not working in a working directory** (sharpening a plan, a design, a piece of writing, anything with no repo under it). If you are in a working directory, use `/grill-with-docs` instead: it runs the same interview and leaves a paper trail, so it is strictly the better one.\n- **`/grilling`** is the interview primitive itself: rounds, the frontier, facts are the agent's job and decisions are yours. `/grill-me` and `/grill-with-docs` are the two named ways in, and `/triage`, `/wayfinder` and `/improve-codebase-architecture` all run it internally. Reach for it directly only when you want the interview with no wrapper around it.\n- **`/resolving-merge-conflicts`** works an in-progress merge or rebase conflict hunk by hunk, resolving by **intent** traced to each side's primary source rather than by picking lines, then finishes the operation. It never runs `--abort`. Standalone and off every flow: reach for it when you are already mid-conflict.\n- **`/prototype`** is a small, throwaway program that answers one design question: does this state model feel right, or what should this UI look like. Throwaway is a constraint on how the code is written, not a promise to destroy it: the answer folds into the real code, and the prototype itself is kept as a **primary source** on a `prototype/<name>` branch out of main, pointed at from the implementation issue. It's the detour in step 2 of the main flow, but reach for it any time a design question is hard to settle on paper.\n- **`/research`**: delegate reading legwork to a **background agent**: it investigates a question against **primary sources**, then leaves a cited Markdown file in the repo. Keep working while it reads. The file it produces is something to take *into* the main flow at `/grill-with-docs`, since research feeds the thinking rather than replacing it.\n- **`/to-questionnaire`** comes in when the thing blocking you isn't in your head or the codebase but in **someone else's**, and it writes them a questionnaire to fill in. It's the inverse of `/grill-me`: instead of interviewing you about the subject, it interviews you about the **send** (who it's going to, what you need back) and aims the questions at the gap. What comes back is material for `/grill-with-docs` or `/to-spec`.\n- **`/wizard`** is for the steps only a **human** can take: provisioning infrastructure, setting up credentials or CI secrets, clicking through an unfamiliar third-party dashboard, running a one-off migration or cutover. It generates an interactive bash script that opens each URL, captures each value, and writes it into `.env` and GitHub secrets, so the procedure stops being something you re-explain to an agent every time. Model-invoked, so the agent reaches for it the moment it hits a wall only you can pass. If the agent could just do it itself, it should; this is for where a human is genuinely in the loop.\n- **`/wait-what`** is the corrective for a message that didn't land. Use it mid-conversation, inside any other skill, and the agent re-pitches what it just said with the context you were missing, in plain English, using the `CONTEXT.md` vocabulary. {"type":"api-request-blob","sessionId":"2cc1b141-f6f4-406d-a6f6-e0223c5e422f","hash":"9b084d5192fcb5803f1bcad64d893ef4c4f6f5e25ca499de098174bf6ce626ae","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"<command-message>mattpocock-skills:ask-matt</command-message>\n<command-name>/mattpocock-skills:ask-matt</command-name>\n<command-args>whats the next stepp to implement the fixes from code review</command-args>\n"},{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: /home/refiv/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/mattpocock-skills/1.2.3/skills/engineering/ask-matt\n\n# Ask Matt\n\nYou don't remember every skill, so ask.\n\nA **flow** is a path through the skills. Most paths run along one **main flow**, and two **on-ramps** merge onto it. Everything else is standalone, or a vocabulary layer that runs underneath.\n\n## The main flow: idea → ship\n\nThe route most work travels. You have an idea and want it built.\n\n1. **`/grill-with-docs`** sharpens the idea by interview. Start here whenever you are **working in a working directory**: it's stateful, retaining what it learns in `CONTEXT.md` and ADRs. (No working directory? Use `/grill-me` instead, covered under Standalone. Both run the same `/grilling` primitive; `grill-with-docs` is the one that leaves a paper trail, which makes it the better of the two whenever a repo is there to leave it in.)\n2. **Branch: can you settle every question in conversation?** If a question needs a runnable answer (state, business logic, a UI you have to see), detour through a prototype, bridged by **`/handoff`** in both directions (a prototype lives in its own directory, which is exactly what `/handoff` is for; see Phase boundaries):\n   - **`/handoff`** out, then open a fresh session against that file,\n   - **`/prototype`** to answer the question with throwaway code,\n   - **`/handoff`** back what you learned, and reference it from the original idea thread.\n3. **Branch: is this a multi-session build?**\n   - **Yes** → **`/to-spec`** (turn the thread into a spec), then **`/to-tickets`** to split it into tracer-bullet tickets, each declaring its **blocking edges**. On a local tracker that's one file per ticket under `.scratch/<feature>/issues/`, worked blockers-first by hand; on a real tracker the edges become native blocking links, so any ticket whose blockers are done can be grabbed: kick off **`/implement`** per ticket, **`/clear`ing context between each one**. Each ticket is self-contained, so the last one's context is disposable.\n   - **No** → **`/implement`** right here, in the same context window.\n\n   Either way, **`/implement`** builds each issue by driving **`/tdd`** internally (one red-green slice at a time), then closes out by running **`/code-review`**, a two-axis review (Standards + Spec) of the diff, before committing. Reach for **`/tdd`** on its own when you just want to build a concrete behaviour test-first without a full spec, and **`/code-review`** on its own whenever you want to review a branch or PR against a fixed point.\n\n### Context hygiene\n\nKeep steps 1–3 in **one unbroken context window** (don't compact or clear until after `/to-tickets`) so the grilling, spec, and tickets all build on the same thinking. Each `/implement` then starts fresh, working from the ticket.\n\nThe limit on this is the **[smart zone](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/smart-zone)**: the window (~150k tokens on state-of-the-art models) within which the model still reasons sharply. If a session approaches it before `/to-tickets`, don't push on degraded; `/compact` at the nearest phase boundary and carry on (see Phase boundaries).\n\n## On-ramps\n\nA starting situation that generates work, then merges onto the main flow.\n\n- **Bugs and requests piling up** → **`/triage`**. It moves issues through triage roles and produces agent-ready issues, which **`/implement`** later picks up.\n\n  Triage is only for issues **you didn't create**: bug reports, incoming feature requests, anything that arrives raw. Tickets that `/to-tickets` produced are already agent-ready, so **don't triage them**.\n\n- **Something's broken** → **`/diagnosing-bugs`**. For the hard ones: the bug that resists a first glance, the intermittent flake, the regression that crept in between two known-good states. It refuses to theorise until it has a **tight feedback loop** (one command that already goes red on *this* bug), then fixes with a regression test. Its post-mortem hands off to **`/improve-codebase-architecture`** when the real finding is that there's no good seam to lock the bug down.\n\n- **A huge, foggy effort: a greenfield project or a huge feature build, too big for one session** → **`/wayfinder`**, the most cognitively demanding flow here. When the way from here to the destination isn't visible yet, it charts a **shared map** of **decision tickets** on the issue tracker and resolves them one at a time, producing **decisions, not deliverables**, until the fog is pushed back and the way is clear. Where **`/grill-with-docs`** sharpens an idea you can hold in one session, wayfinder is for the idea you can't, and it's slower and denser, so save it for exactly that, never a well-scoped feature.\n\n  When the map clears, **it hands off, it doesn't build**: merge onto the main flow at **`/to-spec`**, which collapses the map's linked decisions into a buildable plan, then `/to-tickets` and `/implement` as usual. Looping the map straight into `/implement` skips that collapse and throws the linked detail away, so go straight to `/implement` only when the effort turned out genuinely small.\n\n## Codebase health\n\nNot feature work, just upkeep.\n\n- **`/improve-codebase-architecture`** runs whenever you have a spare moment to keep the codebase good for agents to operate in. It surfaces **deepening opportunities**; picking one _generates an idea_ you can take into the main flow at `/grill-with-docs`. It's the survey that finds the candidates; **`/codebase-design`** (below) is the bench you design the chosen one on.\n\n## Vocabulary underneath\n\nTwo model-invoked references that run *beneath* the other skills, each the single source of truth for its vocabulary. Reach for them directly when the **words**, not the process, are the problem; or let the skills above pull them in.\n\n- **`/domain-modeling`**: sharpen the project's *domain* language: challenge a fuzzy term, resolve an overloaded word (\"account\" doing three jobs), record a hard-to-reverse decision as an ADR. It's the active discipline `/grill-with-docs` drives to keep `CONTEXT.md` a clean glossary.\n- **`/codebase-design`** is the deep-module vocabulary (module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage, locality) for designing a module's *shape*: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface at a clean seam. `/tdd` and `/improve-codebase-architecture` both speak it.\n\n## Phase boundaries\n\nA **phase** is a chunk of work inside a session: the grilling, the implementation, the QA. At the **boundary** between two of them you have five options, and picking between them is the fuzziest decision in this whole map:\n\n- **Continue**: stay put. Costs nothing, loses nothing.\n- **`/clear`**: empty the window, when nothing here matters to what's next.\n- **`/handoff`** writes a portable markdown file. Narrow: only for a **new harness**, a **new directory**, a **colleague**, or forking a side task **mid-phase**. What it buys is portability.\n- **Subagent**: send a tightly-scoped task to its own window and get a report back.\n- **`/compact`** compresses this context and seeds a fresh session with it. The **default**, at the bottom of the tree rather than the first reach.\n\nRead [PHASE-BOUNDARIES.md](PHASE-BOUNDARIES.md) for the ordered tree: the five questions, the reasoning behind each branch, and why the primary-source cost makes **Continue** the one to rule out first. Make the decision **at** a boundary; mid-phase, continue or split the rest into subagents.\n\n## Standalone\n\nOff the main flow entirely.\n\n- **`/grill-me`**: the same relentless interview as `/grill-with-docs`, but **stateless**: it saves nothing locally and builds no `CONTEXT.md`. Reach for it when you are **not working in a working directory** (sharpening a plan, a design, a piece of writing, anything with no repo under it). If you are in a working directory, use `/grill-with-docs` instead: it runs the same interview and leaves a paper trail, so it is strictly the better one.\n- **`/grilling`** is the interview primitive itself: rounds, the frontier, facts are the agent's job and decisions are yours. `/grill-me` and `/grill-with-docs` are the two named ways in, and `/triage`, `/wayfinder` and `/improve-codebase-architecture` all run it internally. Reach for it directly only when you want the interview with no wrapper around it.\n- **`/resolving-merge-conflicts`** works an in-progress merge or rebase conflict hunk by hunk, resolving by **intent** traced to each side's primary source rather than by picking lines, then finishes the operation. It never runs `--abort`. Standalone and off every flow: reach for it when you are already mid-conflict.\n- **`/prototype`** is a small, throwaway program that answers one design question: does this state model feel right, or what should this UI look like. Throwaway is a constraint on how the code is written, not a promise to destroy it: the answer folds into the real code, and the prototype itself is kept as a **primary source** on a `prototype/<name>` branch out of main, pointed at from the implementation issue. It's the detour in step 2 of the main flow, but reach for it any time a design question is hard to settle on paper.\n- **`/research`**: delegate reading legwork to a **background agent**: it investigates a question against **primary sources**, then leaves a cited Markdown file in the repo. Keep working while it reads. The file it produces is something to take *into* the main flow at `/grill-with-docs`, since research feeds the thinking rather than replacing it.\n- **`/to-questionnaire`** comes in when the thing blocking you isn't in your head or the codebase but in **someone else's**, and it writes them a questionnaire to fill in. It's the inverse of `/grill-me`: instead of interviewing you about the subject, it interviews you about the **send** (who it's going to, what you need back) and aims the questions at the gap. What comes back is material for `/grill-with-docs` or `/to-spec`.\n- **`/wizard`** is for the steps only a **human** can take: provisioning infrastructure, setting up credentials or CI secrets, clicking through an unfamiliar third-party dashboard, running a one-off migration or cutover. It generates an interactive bash script that opens each URL, captures each value, and writes it into `.env` and GitHub secrets, so the procedure stops being something you re-explain to an agent every time. Model-invoked, so the agent reaches for it the moment it hits a wall only you can pass. If the agent could just do it itself, it should; this is for where a human is genuinely in the loop.\n- **`/wait-what`** is the corrective for a message that didn't land. Use it mid-conversation, inside any other skill, and the agent re-pitches what it just said with the context you were missing, in plain English, using the `CONTEXT.md` vocabulary. It works after the fact; `/grill-with-docs` is the upfront cure, because a shared language agreed early is what stops the jargon arriving at all.\n- **`/teach`**: learn a concept over multiple sessions, using the current directory as a stateful workspace.\n- **`/writing-for-agents`** is the reference for writing documents agents consume: skills, AGENTS.md, pointed-at docs.\n\n## Precondition\n\n**`/setup-matt-pocock-skills`**: run before your first engineering flow to configure the issue tracker, triage labels, and doc layout the other skills assume. Custom issue trackers also work.\n\n\nARGUMENTS: whats the next stepp to implement the fixes from code review"}]}}

{"parentUuid":"93848306-f3b1-4316-a966-8aa49b457c4a","isSidechain":false,"promptId":"1df7d480-46b0-4d69-aa28-4548c8488ffe","type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: /home/refiv/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/mattpocock-skills/1.2.3/skills/engineering/tdd\n\n# Test-Driven Development\n\nTDD is the red → green loop. This skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle: consult them before and during the loop, not after.\n\nWhen exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.\n\n## What a good test is\n\nTests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely; tests shouldn't. A good test reads like a specification: \"user can checkout with valid cart\" tells you exactly what capability exists, and it survives refactors because it doesn't care about internal structure.\n\nSee [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for mocking guidelines.\n\n## Seams: where tests go\n\nA **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.\n\n**Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything, so agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.\n\nAsk: \"What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?\"\n\nWhen the shape of that interface is itself in question (how deep the module is, where the seam belongs, what the interface should expose), call the Skill tool with \"codebase-design\" for the vocabulary. It is the shared source of the module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage and locality terms, and it is a reference to consult, not a session to run.\n\n## Anti-patterns\n\n- **Implementation-coupled**: mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (querying the database instead of using the interface). The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed.\n- **Tautological**: the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does (`expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`, a snapshot derived by hand the same way, a constant asserted equal to itself), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code. Expected values must come from an independent source of truth: a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.\n- **Horizontal slicing**: writing all tests first, then all implementation. Bulk tests verify _imagined_ behavior: you test the _shape_ of things rather than user-facing behavior, the tests go insensitive to real changes, and you commit to test structure before understanding the implementation. Work in **vertical slices** instead: one test → one implementation → repeat, each test a **tracer bullet** that responds to what the last cycle taught you.\n\n## Rules of the loop\n\n- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.\n- **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.\n- **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.\n\n\nARGUMENTS: Fix the S2 code-review findings. First a failing test in tests/test_login_hardening.py: concurrent wrong-password logins for one email (threads, e.g. 10 at once) get at most 5 responses with 401 and the rest 429. Then make the limiter's check, the password verify and the failure recording happen under a per-email lock in app/login_limiter.py so that test passes. Also: make clear() remove the lockout too; prune expired entries; build LOCKOUT_ERROR from WINDOW; have _key call accounts' email normalizer instead of copying it. Do not add an accounts.authenticate_limited interface. No new dependencies."}]},"isMeta":true,"turnCompanion":true,"uuid":"7d187218-c267-4300-81f1-80c6328e61c8","timestamp":"2026-10-22T00:44:59.384Z","userType":"external","entrypoint":"cli","cwd":"/home/refiv/ubuncode/iphs400-mp2-cms","sessionId":"2cc1b141-f6f4-406d-a6f6-e0223c5e422f","version":"2.1.307","gitBranch":"main"}

Compute the remaining time from _locked_until, or word it as 'up to 15 minutes'.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/login_limiter.py\",\n    \"line\": 34,\n    \"summary\": \"is_locked reads _locked_until without holding _state, while _prune (run from record_failure under a different stripe lock) deletes entries from that same dict.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"Thread A is in is_locked(email1) under stripe 3 while thread B is in record_failure(email2) under stripe 7, pruning _locked_until. On free-threaded CPython (3.13t+), or any later move away from relying on the GIL, the concurrent read and delete can race. The docstring says _state 'guards the two dicts', but this read goes around it.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/login_limiter.py\",\n    \"line\": 39,\n    \"summary\": \"record_failure runs _prune, a full scan of both dicts, on every failed login while holding the global _state lock.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"A script sends wrong logins for N distinct emails within 15 minutes. Each failure is O(N) under one lock, so failure handling grows quadratically overall and blocks every other login's record_failure or clear. Prune only every k calls or past a size threshold, or keep an expiry-ordered deque.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/login_limiter.py\",\n    \"line\": 41,\n    \"summary\": \"Memory is unbounded within the window: every distinct typed email, including made-up ones and the empty string, gets an entry kept for 15 minutes.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"Anyone who can reach /login and repeatedly loads it for a CSRF token can post wrong logins for millions of random emails. _failures and _locked_until grow without limit until the window passes, because pruning drops only expired entries. LOCK_STRIPES caps the locks but not the data.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/routes/auth.py\",\n    \"line\": 27,\n    \"summary\": \"The stripe lock is held across the argon2 verify (deliberately, for the 5-try guarantee), so unrelated emails that hash to the same stripe queue behind each other's slow hash verification.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"An attacker floods guesses for an email that shares a stripe with the Coach's email (1-in-64 chance, which changes per process because Python randomizes string hashes). The Coach's real login waits behind each queued argon2 verification and can feel hung, even though his email is not locked.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"tests/test_login_hardening.py\",\n    \"line\": 92,\n    \"summary\": \"The concurrency test sends from one TestClient in 10 threads at once; its httpx cookie jar and session cookie are not thread-safe.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"Responses that set or rotate the session cookie race on the shared jar. A request may go out with a mismatched session cookie and CSRF token and get a CSRF failure (403/400) instead of 401/429. The exact assertion sorted(statuses) == [401]*5 + [429]*5 then fails now and then.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/login_limiter.py\",\n    \"line\": 50,\n    \"summary\": \"clear() also pops _locked_until, which the route can never need: a successful login only happens after is_locked returned False under the same stripe lock. That branch is used only by a test that calls limiter.clear directly.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"Dead branch in production. It creates an undocumented way to lift a lockout that contradicts CONTEXT.md ('the lockout ends on its own'), and test_clearing_an_email_lifts_its_lockout locks in behavior no caller uses.\"\n  }\n]\n```</result>\n<usage><subagent_tokens>44575</subagent_tokens><tool_uses>2</tool_uses><duration_ms>1070841</duration_ms></usage>\n</task-notification>"}

The user can send it another message and resume it, so the same task-id may notify more than once.</note>\n<result>The review found 7 issues, but none would break a login in normal use. The most serious is a lockout message that can state the wrong wait time. I didn't verify these; per the instructions I only removed duplicates.\n\n```json\n[\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/routes/auth.py\",\n    \"line\": 16,\n    \"summary\": \"LOCKOUT_ERROR always says 'Try again in 15 minutes', whatever time is actually left on the lockout.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"Editor gets locked out, then tries again 14 minutes later and gets a 429 that still says 'Try again in 15 minutes' (the frozen-clock test shows it). The user is told to wait far longer than needed and loses trust in the message. Compute the remaining time from _locked_until, or word it as 'up to 15 minutes'.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/login_limiter.py\",\n    \"line\": 34,\n    \"summary\": \"is_locked reads _locked_until without holding _state, while _prune (run from record_failure under a different stripe lock) deletes entries from that same dict.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"Thread A is in is_locked(email1) under stripe 3 while thread B is in record_failure(email2) under stripe 7, pruning _locked_until. On free-threaded CPython (3.13t+), or any later move away from relying on the GIL, the concurrent read and delete can race. The docstring says _state 'guards the two dicts', but this read goes around it.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/login_limiter.py\",\n    \"line\": 39,\n    \"summary\": \"record_failure runs _prune, a full scan of both dicts, on every failed login while holding the global _state lock.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"A script sends wrong logins for N distinct emails within 15 minutes. Each failure is O(N) under one lock, so failure handling grows quadratically overall and blocks every other login's record_failure or clear. Prune only every k calls or past a size threshold, or keep an expiry-ordered deque.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/login_limiter.py\",\n    \"line\": 41,\n    \"summary\": \"Memory is unbounded within the window: every distinct typed email, including made-up ones and the empty string, gets an entry kept for 15 minutes.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"Anyone who can reach /login and repeatedly loads it for a CSRF token can post wrong logins for millions of random emails. _failures and _locked_until grow without limit until the window passes, because pruning drops only expired entries. LOCK_STRIPES caps the locks but not the data.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/routes/auth.py\",\n    \"line\": 27,\n    \"summary\": \"The stripe lock is held across the argon2 verify (deliberately, for the 5-try guarantee), so unrelated emails that hash to the same stripe queue behind each other's slow hash verification.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"An attacker floods guesses for an email that shares a stripe with the Coach's email (1-in-64 chance, which changes per process because Python randomizes string hashes). The Coach's real login waits behind each queued argon2 verification and can feel hung, even though his email is not locked.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"tests/test_login_hardening.py\",\n    \"line\": 92,\n    \"summary\": \"The concurrency test sends from one TestClient in 10 threads at once; its httpx cookie jar and session cookie are not thread-safe.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"Responses that set or rotate the session cookie race on the shared jar. A request may go out with a mismatched session cookie and CSRF token and get a CSRF failure (403/400) instead of 401/429. The exact assertion sorted(statuses) == [401]*5 + [429]*5 then fails now and then.\"\n  },\n  {\n    \"file\": \"app/login_limiter.py\",\n    \"line\": 50,\n    \"summary\": \"clear() also pops _locked_until, which the route can never need: a successful login only happens after is_locked returned False under the same stripe lock. That branch is used only by a test that calls limiter.clear directly.\",\n    \"failure_scenario\": \"Dead branch in production. It creates an undocumented way to lift a lockout that contradicts CONTEXT.md ('the lockout ends on its own'), and test_clearing_an_email_lifts_its_lockout locks in behavior no caller uses.\"\n  }\n]\n```</result>\n<usage><subagent_tokens>44575</subagent_tokens><tool_uses>2</tool_uses><duration_ms>1070841</duration_ms></usage>\n</task-notification>"},"uuid":"2257aaa0-6d14-4278-bbfb-38caf87ee0ec","timestamp":"2026-10-22T01:30:34.228Z","permissionMode":"auto","origin":{"kind":"task-notification","producer":"session-task","runId":"0mviujops-c4cb387c"},"promptSource":"system","turnOrigin":"task_notification","turnPosition":{"promptIndex":4,"turnIndex":6},"queueSkipAttachments":true,"userType":"external","entrypoint":"cli","cwd":"/home/refiv/ubuncode/iphs400-mp2-cms","sessionId":"2cc1b141-f6f4-406d-a6f6-e0223c5e422f","version":"2.1.307","gitBranch":"main"}

{"parentUuid":"a33b3b6e-11d9-4521-a131-e8a504a0133c","isSidechain":false,"promptId":"7c09a148-0b84-4c8b-b648-3bf3a4948a1c","type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: /home/refiv/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/mattpocock-skills/1.2.3/skills/engineering/tdd\n\n# Test-Driven Development\n\nTDD is the red → green loop. This skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle: consult them before and during the loop, not after.\n\nWhen exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.\n\n## What a good test is\n\nTests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely; tests shouldn't. A good test reads like a specification: \"user can checkout with valid cart\" tells you exactly what capability exists, and it survives refactors because it doesn't care about internal structure.\n\nSee [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for mocking guidelines.\n\n## Seams: where tests go\n\nA **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.\n\n**Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything, so agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.\n\nAsk: \"What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?\"\n\nWhen the shape of that interface is itself in question (how deep the module is, where the seam belongs, what the interface should expose), call the Skill tool with \"codebase-design\" for the vocabulary. It is the shared source of the module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage and locality terms, and it is a reference to consult, not a session to run.\n\n## Anti-patterns\n\n- **Implementation-coupled**: mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (querying the database instead of using the interface). The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed.\n- **Tautological**: the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does (`expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`, a snapshot derived by hand the same way, a constant asserted equal to itself), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code. Expected values must come from an independent source of truth: a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.\n- **Horizontal slicing**: writing all tests first, then all implementation. Bulk tests verify _imagined_ behavior: you test the _shape_ of things rather than user-facing behavior, the tests go insensitive to real changes, and you commit to test structure before understanding the implementation. Work in **vertical slices** instead: one test → one implementation → repeat, each test a **tracer bullet** that responds to what the last cycle taught you.\n\n## Rules of the loop\n\n- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.\n- **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.\n- **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.\n\n\nARGUMENTS: proceed with fixes 1 and 2, check 6, revert 7"}]},"isMeta":true,"turnCompanion":true,"uuid":"b9ca85ff-c01e-4429-b4aa-2e887a5e365a","timestamp":"2026-10-22T01:32:51.483Z","userType":"external","entrypoint":"cli","cwd":"/home/refiv/ubuncode/iphs400-mp2-cms","sessionId":"2cc1b141-f6f4-406d-a6f6-e0223c5e422f","version":"2.1.307","gitBranch":"main"}

No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything, so agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.\n\nAsk: \"What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?\"\n\nWhen the shape of that interface is itself in question (how deep the module is, where the seam belongs, what the interface should expose), call the Skill tool with \"codebase-design\" for the vocabulary. It is the shared source of the module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage and locality terms, and it is a reference to consult, not a session to run.\n\n## Anti-patterns\n\n- **Implementation-coupled**: mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (querying the database instead of using the interface). The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed.\n- **Tautological**: the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does (`expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`, a snapshot derived by hand the same way, a constant asserted equal to itself), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code. Expected values must come from an independent source of truth: a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.\n- **Horizontal slicing**: writing all tests first, then all implementation. Bulk tests verify _imagined_ behavior: you test the _shape_ of things rather than user-facing behavior, the tests go insensitive to real changes, and you commit to test structure before understanding the implementation. Work in **vertical slices** instead: one test → one implementation → repeat, each test a **tracer bullet** that responds to what the last cycle taught you.\n\n## Rules of the loop\n\n- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.\n- **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.\n- **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.\n\n\nARGUMENTS: proceed with fixes 1 and 2, check 6, revert 7"}]}}
